rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window of all 10 compounds while minimizing truncation risk. The retention and resolution pattern will guide window trimming and targeted slope or temperature tests.

Halve the gradient time to test how much the current resolution margin can be traded for a shorter run. Keeping the window and temperature fixed isolates the effect of gradient slope on the critical pairs.
Test a substantial temperature shift at the faster gradient to change selectivity within the crowded middle group. Higher temperature should also shorten retention, preserving the zero time penalty.

Use a slightly shallower gradient and intermediate temperature to separate the crowded middle peaks without the near-coelution seen at 60 C. The last peak should remain near the zero-time-penalty window.

Raise temperature by 5 C to open the remaining close middle pair while retaining the resolution gained with the 12-minute gradient. This should also keep the last peak below the time-penalty threshold.

Injection 5 already achieved the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Test a slightly higher starting organic fraction to seek another maximum-scoring method with a shorter run, while checking that early peaks remain retained and resolved.

Keep injection 5 as the maximum-scoring benchmark and test a slightly shallower gradient for improved resolution margin. Restoring the lower starting organic fraction protects the pair that deteriorated in injection 6.

The maximum CRF is already secured by injection 5. Test the faster gradient at lower temperature to explore an alternative selectivity regime that might resolve the middle cluster while retaining a zero time penalty.

Slightly flatten injection 6's gradient to improve its limiting pair while preserving the separation of the other close pair. This may yield another maximum-scoring method with a better resolution margin; injection 5 remains the benchmark.

Reduce the gradient slope one more grid step to raise the limiting resolution above 1.5, while the other close pair should remain resolved. The last peak is expected near 8 minutes, potentially preserving the maximum CRF with a slightly better resolution margin.

The maximum score is already secured, so test a substantially steeper gradient at 60 C for a faster alternative selectivity regime. The close pair seen at this temperature may separate after an elution-order reversal, although other pairs could become compressed.

Test a two-minute reduction from the maximum-scoring injection 5 while holding its successful temperature and solvent window fixed. This directly checks whether full resolution can be retained in a faster run; the established maximum-scoring methods remain the fallback.

Match injection 5's successful gradient slope while trimming the unused high-organic portion of the gradient. All peaks should elute before the gradient ends, preserving the maximum CRF with a lower final organic fraction.

Test a slope between injections 9 and 10 to balance their two limiting pairs while keeping the last peak below 8 minutes. The final organic fraction remains comfortably above the estimated last-peak elution fraction.

Test whether a higher starting fraction combined with a shallower gradient improves the resolution margin around the maximum-scoring region. Monitor early-peak retention and the last-peak time; the established CRF 1.000 methods remain the benchmark.

With the maximum CRF already secured, explore a faster alternative using higher temperature and starting organic fraction to move the troublesome middle pair beyond its selectivity crossover. Check whether that pair opens without sacrificing early-peak resolution.

Increase the starting organic fraction one grid step from injection 16 to test whether its remaining close pair separates further. Early-peak compression is the main risk; the previously achieved CRF 1.000 remains the campaign benchmark.

Return to the successful 55 C region and test a slightly shallower slope than injection 10 to assess the resolution-versus-time boundary. The maximum CRF is already secured; this run checks whether additional separation margin is available before the time penalty becomes significant.

Lengthen injection 15's gradient to test whether its limiting pair reaches baseline resolution while preserving the stronger separation of the other critical pair. This explores additional resolution margin, with the established CRF 1.000 methods retained if the longer run incurs a time penalty.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 19 to improve its limiting resolution and balance the two closest pairs. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, potentially preserving CRF 1.000 with a larger separation margin.
Test a slope between injections 19 and 20 to balance the two limiting resolutions near 1.7. This should retain the maximum CRF while slightly shortening retention relative to injection 20.

Trim the gradient endpoint while closely matching injection 21's slope and balanced resolution. The last peak is expected around 9.3 minutes, before the gradient ends, so this lower-organic method should preserve CRF 1.000.

Test the lower-temperature boundary of injection 22's maximum-scoring method while keeping its gradient fixed. This measures temperature sensitivity of the balanced middle pairs; the established 55 C methods already secure the highest possible CRF.

Test the upper-temperature boundary of injection 22 to complete the local selectivity comparison. This will establish whether 55 C is uniquely favorable on the available temperature grid; the maximum campaign score is already secured.

Trim the successful injection 5 gradient to a lower endpoint while preserving its starting fraction, slope, and temperature. All peaks should elute before the gradient ends, reproducing the maximum CRF with less high-organic exposure.
